title: The Man Who Lost His Brakes
synopsis: Tom Hayes, a long-haul truck driver, arrives in the ED tremulous and hallucinating after a hard stop on I-80. His brain, chronically suppressed by whiskey, is now running without its main braking system — and with a history of DTs, this withdrawal is accelerating fast.

chapters.heading: Disruption
chapters.body: Tom Hayes stumbles through the ED doors, his partner half-carrying him. His hands shake so badly he can't unzip his jacket — he keeps slapping at his own arms and neck, muttering about ants crawling on the curtains. The triage nurse takes vitals: pulse 90, blood pressure 101/64, SpO₂ hovering at 93%. He hasn't had a drink since yesterday morning, and his body is already screaming for it.
chapters.visualHint: Wide 3/4 shot: Tom in the triage bay, jacket half-off, one hand batting at his neck, partner steadying him. Fluorescent lights overhead, curtain behind.

chapters.heading: Embodiment
chapters.body: Dr. Oppong kneels beside the bed and watches Tom's eyes dart to the corner of the room — he's tracking something that isn't there. His skin is slick with sweat, and when the doctor asks him to hold out his hands, the tremor is coarse and constant. Tom's brain has been running on a liter of whiskey a day for years; the GABA receptors are suppressed, the brakes are off, and the sympathetic nervous system is surging unchecked.
chapters.visualHint: Medium close-up: Dr. Oppong's face in foreground, Tom's trembling hands extended, sweat on his brow, eyes wide and unfocused.

chapters.heading: Escalation
chapters.body: The nurse starts a CIWA-Ar assessment, and Tom's score climbs past 15 — severe withdrawal. His heart rate ticks up to 110, his blood pressure edges higher, and he begins to pick at the sheets, convinced the ants are crawling up his legs. This is the kindled brain of a man who has been through delirium tremens before; each episode primes the next to hit harder and faster.
chapters.visualHint: Over-the-shoulder of nurse holding CIWA-Ar clipboard, Tom in bed gripping the sheet, monitor showing HR 110, BP 108/70.

chapters.heading: Crisis point
chapters.body: Tom's agitation spikes — he tries to climb off the bed, shouting that the ants are in his mouth. The nurse calls for help, and Dr. Oppong orders IV lorazepam, titrating to sedation but keeping him arousable. Without the benzodiazepine to restore GABA tone, the autonomic storm could tip into seizures or full-blown delirium tremens, where the fever climbs and the heart races until the patient crashes.
chapters.visualHint: Medium shot: two nurses holding Tom's arms as he strains upward, Dr. Oppong at the bedside with a syringe, monitor alarm flashing.

chapters.heading: Mechanism turn
chapters.body: As the lorazepam takes hold, Tom's tremor softens, his breathing slows, and he sinks back into the pillow. The doctor explains to the team: alcohol chronically suppresses GABA, the brain's main brake. When the alcohol disappears, the brake is gone — the sympathetic system runs wild. The benzodiazepine is a temporary replacement brake, buying time to correct electrolytes, give thiamine, and prevent Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome before glucose hits his system.
chapters.visualHint: Close-up: Dr. Oppong's hand adjusting the IV drip, Tom's face relaxing, eyes closing, monitor showing HR 90, BP 100/65.

chapters.heading: Recontextualization
chapters.body: Tom is admitted to the ICU for continuous CIWA monitoring and IV benzodiazepines. The team consults addiction medicine — this relapse after job loss carries a risk of deliberate overdose, and a safety assessment is needed. But for now, the immediate crisis is contained. His brain, once running without brakes, has a temporary governor. The real work — detox, rehab, mood support — begins when the autonomic storm passes.
chapters.visualHint: Wide shot: Tom asleep in ICU bed, IV lines, monitor with stable vitals, a nurse adjusting the pump, daylight through the window.

masterImagePrompt: A 45-year-old white male in a hospital gown, lying in an ED bed, tremulous and diaphoretic, one hand raised as if brushing something off his neck. IV line in his arm, cardiac monitor on the wall showing HR 110. Fluorescent lighting, curtain behind. No overhead bird's-eye view.
patientLock: 45-year-old white male, hospital gown, disheveled, sweaty, tremulous — consistent across all chapters.
